delta_name: Congestion character: channel routing → pin access
at_28nm: Congestion was primarily about macro channels and global routing track saturation; spreading cells and widening channels usually relieved it. Pin access at the standard cell boundary was relatively forgiving because cells were 9-12 track tall with multiple M1/M2 access options.
at_7nm_5nm: Congestion is dominated by pin access. Standard cells are 6-track or shorter, M1 pin landing is geometrically starved, and SADP/SAQP coloring rules make small jogs extremely expensive. A region can have 65% utilization and still be unroutable because the router cannot physically reach cell pins.
why_it_changed: SADP/SAQP mandate parallel-running metal lines; any turn consumes an additional metal layer plus vias, multiplying via resistance. To hit density targets, libraries are 'scrunched' to 6-track/5-track, collapsing the number of M1 pin slots per cell. The bottleneck moves from 'space between macros' to 'the cell boundary itself'.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer sees congestion, applies cell spreading / density screens expecting the overflow to clear — but at 7nm the overflow persists or worsens because the real problem is pin access, not cell density. Observable symptom: global route shows modest overflow, yet detailed route produces massive DRC counts concentrated exactly at cell boundaries, not in channels. Weeks are wasted spreading cells before someone runs a pin-access report.
workflow_impact: Pin-access analysis and legalization quality checks move to early placement (pre-CTS), not just post-route. Library selection (pin-access-friendly cell variants) and placement legalizer tuning become first-class steps.

delta_name: Timing driver: cell delay → interconnect + via resistance
at_28nm: On average, cell delay and net delay each contributed to the overall path delay. When fixing setup violations, the common practice was to upsize/downgrade-Vt the cells on the path, which often improved timing because the cell contribution was substantial.
at_7nm_5nm: Interconnect resistance (and via resistance) dominate. Wire delay increasingly overshadows cell delay. Buffering and layer assignment matter more than swapping a cell. A path that is a few picoseconds short may be fixed by a path-based analysis (PBA) run before touching the design, because graph-based analysis is pessimistic.
why_it_changed: Wire resistance scales up as metal pitches shrink. Vias become a real resistance bottleneck. At the same time, lower Vdd (approaching 0.5-0.7V) reduces noise margins. The challenge is further compounded by increased variation and the need for yield-aware design.
what_breaks: An engineer accustomed to 28nm tries to fix a 7nm setup violation by upsizing cells or swapping Vt — area and power grow, but timing barely improves because the net delay component is now the bottleneck. Observable symptom: cell delay % in the path report is <30%, net delay is >70%, yet the team keeps upsizing cells. They should have re-buffered, reassigned layers, or restructured the path.
workflow_impact: Layer assignment and buffer insertion optimization become central to timing closure; PBA becomes a standard step before any design change. Extraction correlation (trial-route RC vs. signoff RC) is far more critical.

at_28nm: Flat OCV derates or AOCV with distance-based derating were adequate. A single derate number per arc captured enough pessimism/optimism; timing signoff across PVT corners was tractable.
at_7nm_5nm: Local variation between neighboring cells is significant. Variation in delay can become larger than nominal delay at lower voltages. Advanced flows move to statistical models like POCV, using per-cell sigma data from LVF libraries, to model variation accurately instead of guessing a worst case.
why_it_changed: Transistors are so small that Random Dopant Fluctuations (RDF), Line Edge Roughness (LER), and work function variation cause large local variation. Flat OCV is dangerously optimistic (hides variation-induced escapes) or grossly pessimistic (over-constrains). Statistical POCV is mandatory for accurate signoff.
what_breaks: Team ships using flat OCV at 7nm/5nm because 'that's what we've always done'. Two observable outcomes: (a) chip passes STA but fails in silicon across slow-lot corners (under-pessimistic), or (b) timing never closes and they burn months over-optimizing (over-pessimistic). Either way, the STA numbers are not trustworthy. Conversely, running POCV on a 28nm design adds runtime and LVF library cost for negligible benefit.
workflow_impact: POCV/LVF library procurement and characterization become part of the node bring-up. STA tool configuration switches from derate-based to statistical. Runtime explodes due to more corners/scenarios.

at_28nm: A handful of corners (best-case, typical, worst-case, perhaps one extra for low-voltage) were sufficient. MCMM setup was light.
at_7nm_5nm: Dozens of corners and modes are mandatory. At 5nm, because of the overall thermal envelope and power consumption budget, designs are running all corners at sub-600 millivolts. Combined with more timing and power scenarios, design cycles lengthen considerably.
why_it_changed: Lower Vdd magnifies variation sensitivity, near-threshold operation changes the worst-case corner, and the sheer number of operating modes (DVFS states, power gates, multiple clock domains) multiplies the scenario matrix. Interconnect RC parasitic variation compounds this, requiring tighter corners.
what_breaks: A team closing timing on a subset of 'representative' corners, assuming the others will follow. Observable symptom: chip passes STA on 8 corners but fails in the field at a 9th corner that was deprioritized. At 5nm, missing a sub-500mV NTC corner is fatal because that IS the operating condition. The mistake is treating corner selection as a runtime optimization rather than a signoff completeness requirement.
workflow_impact: MCMM scenario definition becomes a dedicated signoff task with foundry guidance. EDA capacity/license planning must account for 5-10x runtime growth. Early definition of the full corner matrix is critical to avoid painful re-closure.

at_28nm: Most critical layers were single-patterned (DUV). Coloring was not a placement/routing concern for digital logic. Design rules were comparatively relaxed.
at_7nm_5nm: Multi-patterning (SADP/SAQP) is mandatory on critical metal layers; EUV reduces but does not eliminate it. Layout must be coloring-aware; full coloring is required. Preferred mask assignment for critical nets affects performance.
why_it_changed: Optical lithography resolution limits require splitting a layer into two or more masks. Coloring rules constrain which adjacent shapes can be on the same mask. EUV helps at 5nm for some layers but does not eliminate multi-patterning entirely.
what_breaks: Engineer places cells/routes wires ignoring coloring constraints, expecting DRC to catch them later. Observable symptom: thousands of coloring violations (same-mask spacing) surface in physical verification; fixing them requires re-placement or re-routing because the violations are structural. Physical verification (DRC) iteration count jumps from 1-2 to 4-5 runs.
workflow_impact: Coloring-aware placement and routing become part of the mainstream flow; physical verification (DRC) iteration count jumps. Foundry DRC decks are substantially more complex (25-30% more checks per node).

delta_name: Power grid vs. standard cell co-design (IR/EM first-class)
at_28nm: Power grid could be designed somewhat independently of standard cells; IR drop was a post-route check, and EM was often a final signoff checkbox. Grid pitch/width were chosen with reasonable heuristics.
at_7nm_5nm: The standard cell architecture must fit with the power grid; they must be co-designed. At 5nm, IR drop and EM issues are nearly impossible to resolve if this interaction isn't accounted for from the beginning. Via and metal resistances increase as we shrink to 5nm, requiring a regular, evenly distributed power grid.
why_it_changed: Lower Vdd (sub-600mV operation) means IR drop margin shrinks to ~3% of Vdd at advanced nodes versus ~5% at 28nm. Metal resistance is roughly 10x higher. Simultaneous switching noise (di/dt) induces larger voltage droops. EM limits tighten with smaller vias.
what_breaks: Team builds the power grid using 28nm heuristics (similar strap pitch scaled down) — grid is structurally inadequate but passes early static IR. Observable symptom: post-route dynamic IR drop exceeds budget; EM violations appear on power vias; the fix requires grid re-floorplanning which invalidates placement. At 5nm, the interaction between standard cell architecture and power grid must be considered from the beginning, otherwise it's nearly impossible to resolve.
workflow_impact: Power grid exploration and IR/EM signoff move to early floorplan, tightly coupled with library selection. Dynamic IR with realistic switching vectors becomes mandatory, not just static IR. Vector selection for EM/IR analysis becomes a discipline in itself.

delta_name: Signal integrity (crosstalk) becomes first-order, not a corner case
at_28nm: Crosstalk was a secondary effect; SI-enabled signoff was optional for many designs. Aggressor/victim coupling could often be ignored or covered by clock uncertainty guardbands.
at_7nm_5nm: Wires are packed closer, so capacitive coupling between neighbors is large. Signoff with SI enabled is mandatory. A path that is clean without crosstalk can fail with it on.
why_it_changed: Wire spacing shrinks dramatically while switching speeds increase (3-4GHz). A switching aggressor injects delta delay onto its victim. The coupling capacitance relative to total load grows.
what_breaks: Team signs off timing without SI at 7nm/5nm, then sees functional failures or at-speed test failures in silicon that STA never predicted. Observable symptom: the same RTL that passed STA fails on ATE at high toggle rates; root cause is crosstalk-induced delta delay on critical paths. Conversely, enabling SI for the first time at signoff can produce a flood of violations that should have been caught in placement.
workflow_impact: SI-aware timing becomes part of every sign-off STA run; placement must consider wire spacing for critical nets; NDR with shielding becomes common for high-speed clocks and critical signals.

at_28nm: Target overall utilization of ~70-75% was standard, with localized regions allowed up to 80-85%. Placement had reasonable freedom to spread cells and still meet density.
at_7nm_5nm: Effective utilization must drop to roughly 55-65% because pin access and coloring rules consume a disproportionate amount of space. The 'scrunched' cell architecture means that a nominally 70%-utilized block may be unroutable; the actual placed density must be lower to leave routing tracks and pin-access slots.
why_it_changed: Smaller cells (6-track/5-track) have fewer pin slots; SADP/SAQP rules forbid certain track patterns; multi-patterning coloring forces spacing. The geometric efficiency of placement decreases even if the cell count density looks similar.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer sets the target density at 75% because that's what worked before. Observable symptom: placement completes, but global route overflow is non-zero in regions that look 'only' 75% utilized. Detail route cannot legalize. The team iteratively drops density but loses weeks because the initial target was fundamentally wrong for the node. At 5nm, the combination of tighter pin access and coloring makes this even more pronounced.
workflow_impact: Density planning becomes node-specific and is validated early with trial routes. Floorplan must allocate more white space. The trade-off between area (higher density) and routability (lower density) is far more sensitive.

delta_name: Hold closure difficulty: from easy to hard
at_28nm: Hold violations were relatively easy to fix by inserting delay cells on the data path. The margin between best-case and worst-case was manageable.
at_7nm_5nm: Hold closure becomes significantly harder. Near-threshold operation (sub-500mV at 5nm) means variation in delay can exceed nominal delay. Low voltage magnifies the impact of variation, making it difficult to guarantee hold across all operating conditions. Useful skew, which helps setup, directly costs hold margin.
why_it_changed: At lower Vdd, the ratio of variation to nominal delay increases. A few picoseconds of useful skew applied for setup can tip a hold check into violation under fast-corner/low-voltage conditions. Additionally, the smaller timing windows leave less room for data-path delay insertion.
what_breaks: Engineer applies aggressive useful skew to close setup at 7nm/5nm, then sees a wave of hold violations post-CTS that cannot be fixed without sacrificing the setup gains. Observable symptom: setup is clean, but hold slack is deeply negative on the same paths where skew was applied. Data-path hold buffers cost power and area and may not be sufficient at the fast corner. The team ends up in an iterative loop.
workflow_impact: Hold-aware useful skew (simultaneous setup/hold optimization) becomes mandatory in CTS. Multi-corner hold signoff (especially FF/low-Vdd) is required. The balance between setup and hold optimization is a first-class CTS objective.
